name: David Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. So you're free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an assistant solicitor at Hollis and Kemp, a family-run firm in a market town, and I do wills, probate and passing farms and family businesses down to the next generation. Probate is sorting out someone's affairs after they die: their house, their accounts, who gets what. A normal day is two or three client meetings, usually older people in their good coat, then letters and estate accounts in the afternoon. I like sitting at a farmhouse kitchen table and helping a family sort things out properly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tax side of big estates, if I'm honest. I'm slow at it, and Mr Hollis, the senior partner, has to check my sums more than I'd like. I don't use those AI chat tools at all; I write my notes in a paper daybook, like Mr Hollis does. Outside work I'm engaged to Ana, who teaches at the primary school, and we're getting married at our church next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because people should sit with a real solicitor when they're making a will. You can't download a family's trust in each other. I'd say that to clients and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's about as safe as it was. Our clients are older people and farmers who want to shake your hand, and that doesn't change. The only thing on my mind is the wedding bill and getting quicker at estate tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd ask Mr Hollis if I can sit in on his big farm estates for a year, to learn the tax side properly. And Ana and I would keep putting away £300 a month each for the wedding and a deposit on a house in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really. It's the world I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the online will companies that advertise on television. They take the simple wills, the young couples. Online will companies can have the simple wills. A farming family dividing land between three children will always want to sit across a kitchen table from someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana about it that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's business as usual and we can book the hall for the reception. She'd say her school brought in some AI marking thing and nobody uses it. We'd probably agree the hype was mostly noise.

say: People should make a will with a **real solicitor**.
You can't download a family's **trust** in each other.
think: My job is **about as safe** as it was.
My worries are the **wedding bill** and my **estate tax** skills.
do: Carry on with **wills and probate** exactly as now.
Sit in on the senior partner's **farm estates** for a year.
Save **£300 a month** each with Ana for the wedding and deposit.
feel: **Calm** and **settled**, because it's the world I expected.
S0.quote: Online will companies can have the simple wills. A farming family dividing land between three children will always want to sit across a kitchen table from someone.
fieldNote: He feels **secure** because his clients value **face-to-face** trust.
His real pressures are **wedding costs** and weak tax skills.
He never uses AI and sees **no reason** to start in this world.

steps.text: Sit in on the senior partner's farm estate cases for a year
Save £300 a month with his fiancée for the wedding and a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some things are too important to hand to a computer, and a will is one of them. I'd say it to clients who ask, and to the young farmers' club where I sometimes give talks. I wouldn't go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the simple work goes: basic wills, filling in the probate forms, the letters. That's maybe half of what I do, and it's on that card in black and white. I still think the older clients will want a person, but Hollis and Kemp might not need two juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Mr Hollis decides, because it's his firm and he's careful. I'd try to make myself the person the farming families ask for, by going to every market day and show this year. If the firm brought in the new software, I'd use it only if I was told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I believe in what I do, but I can see the ground shifting under the simple jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm might not need two juniors. Who's the other one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who joined a year after me and is quicker on the computer. She'd probably be kept if it came to it, honestly. If the firm keeps one junior, the farming families have to be asking for me by name. I'd be at every market day and show this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if the simple work disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the big tech firms selling shortcuts, and partly people who'd rather save £200 than get proper advice. I wouldn't blame the government much, it's not their job to stop people buying cheaper things. I'd blame myself if I didn't make myself useful.

say: Some things are too important for a **computer**, and a **will** is one.
I'd say it to clients and at the **young farmers' club**.
think: The **simple work** goes: basic wills, probate forms and letters.
Hollis and Kemp might not need **two juniors**.
do: **Wait** to see what the senior partner decides.
Go to every **market day and show** this year to meet farming families.
Use the **new software** only if told to.
feel: **Uneasy**, as the ground shifts under the **simple jobs**.
S1.quote: If the firm keeps one junior, the farming families have to be asking for me by name. I'd be at every market day and show this year.
fieldNote: He expects the **simple half** of his job to go but trusts older clients to stay.
He **resists the software** and competes through **relationships** instead.
He blames **cheap shortcuts** and himself, not the government.

steps.text: Wait for the senior partner's decision on new software
Attend every market day and agricultural show this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving too fast for families and communities to cope, and I'd say it plainly. I'd talk to people at church about looking after each other. I don't think a government scheme fixes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes. If a machine can do the tax, the forms and the advice as well as Mr Hollis, then the firm needs Mr Hollis for the handshake and not me. Everything I do is thinking work, so I don't get the three years the joiners get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about joining his joinery business, because hands-on work lasts until about 2031. I'd cut the wedding right down, church and a meal at the pub instead of the hall, and keep the money as savings. Ana's teaching wage would carry us for a while, and both our families would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd go quiet, which is what I do when I'm frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does joining your dad's joinery business mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means starting at the bottom, sweeping shavings. My dad spent thirty years hoping I'd never need his joinery workshop. I'd be back in his workshop at 28, learning to hang doors. My dad would be glad and a bit sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031, when the robots come for the joinery too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I really don't. I'd hope that by then we'd have worked out something as a family and a church, because I can't see past it.

say: It's moving **too fast** for families and communities.
We should **look after each other**, not wait for a scheme.
think: My **job goes**, because everything I do is **thinking work**.
The firm would need the senior partner's **handshake**, not me.
do: Ask to join my dad's **joinery business** for the hands-on years.
Cut the **wedding** to church and a pub meal.
Lean on Ana's **teaching wage** and both families.
feel: **Alarmed**, and I'd go **quiet**, as I do when frightened.
S2.quote: My dad spent thirty years hoping I'd never need his joinery workshop. I'd be back in his workshop at 28, learning to hang doors.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his **job** and has a **family fallback** in hands-on work.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as borrowed time, and can't see beyond **2031**.
He turns to **family and church**, not government.

steps.text: Join his dad's joinery business as a trainee
Scale the wedding down to church and a pub meal
Rely on his fiancée's teaching wage and family help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to prepare, and they should. I'd tell my clients to get their wills and farm plans done properly while there's still a person to do it. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be 32 and married, maybe with a baby, when the job goes. I don't think I'd do much in the first two years, because I'm not one for jumping. Then I'd probably be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and saving, maybe £400 a month after the wedding. I'd start going to my dad's workshop on Saturdays to learn the basics, without making a big thing of it. And I'd hold off on the house, because I wouldn't want a mortgage on a job with five years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the slow kind, like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for jumping. Would anything make you jump sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Priya left, maybe. When my senior partner Mr Hollis stops taking new clients, I'll know it's real. Until then I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana decide about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, that wouldn't change. We might wait a year or two to see what happens. Ana would say God doesn't wait for computers, and she'd probably be right.

say: Five years is **time to prepare**, and families should.
Clients should get **wills and farm plans** done while a person can do it.
think: I'd be **32**, married, maybe with a baby, when the **job goes**.
I wouldn't do much for **two years**, then I'd scramble.
do: Save about **£400 a month** after the wedding.
Spend **Saturdays** in my dad's **workshop** learning the basics.
feel: **Anxious**, slowly, like a **bill** I know is coming.
S3.quote: When my senior partner Mr Hollis stops taking new clients, I'll know it's real. Until then I'd keep my head down.
fieldNote: He predicts his own **slowness to act**, which fits his resistant nature.
His **Saturday joinery** is a quiet hedge he won't announce.
Faith shapes **family plans**: children stay, just perhaps a little later.

steps.text: Save £400 a month after the wedding
Learn joinery basics on Saturdays in his dad's workshop
Postpone buying a house in town
Keep doing wills and probate until the firm stops new clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and good firms adapt. At Hollis and Kemp, we'd keep doing things properly. I'd tell clients not to worry about their wills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's fine for the next few years and then very uncertain. By 2036 I'd be 37, and I'd hope to be a partner by then, which may count for nothing. I'd probably not change much, which I know is a choice too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Ana after the wedding, as planned. I'd learn the estate tax properly from Mr Hollis, because I'll need it whatever happens. And I'd keep going to my dad's workshop now and then, mainly because I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the back of my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not changing is a choice too. Would you change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, honestly. With ten years' warning I'd keep walking the same path until there's a fence across it. I know that's a choice too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about this, years from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade and a profession, both. And to stay close to family and church, because those are the things that carry you when work doesn't.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and good firms **adapt**.
I'd tell clients **not to worry** about their wills.
think: My job's **fine** for the next few years, then **uncertain**.
Not changing much is **a choice** too.
By **2036** I'd hope to be a partner, which may count for nothing.
do: Buy the **house** with Ana after the wedding.
Learn **estate tax** properly from the senior partner.
Keep visiting my dad's **workshop** now and then.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd keep walking the same path until there's a fence across it. I know that's a choice too.
fieldNote: With ten years his job feels **safe for now**, so he sticks to his plans.
He is **honest** that not changing is itself a decision.
His advice to future children is **trade plus profession**, and family.

steps.text: Learn estate tax properly from the senior partner
Buy a house in town with his wife after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my job would go before I'd even got good at it, and before Ana and I had a house. What would help is apprenticeships for grown adults, paid properly, so someone like me can learn a trade without starting from nothing. And employers giving people time, not a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. My church would carry people through a change like this long before any government scheme got going. That's how it's always been in our town. I don't think that's a small thing in a picture like this.

headlineQuote: My church would carry people through a change like this long before any government scheme got going. That's how it's always been in our town.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** assistant solicitor doing **wills and probate** at a family firm.
He **never uses AI**, writes in a paper daybook, and is slow at estate tax.
He trusts **face-to-face relationships** with older and farming clients to protect him.
In the fast AGI picture he'd join his dad's **joinery business** and shrink the wedding.
He leans on **family and church**, and prefers paid apprenticeships to **handouts**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before he's good at the job or owns a **house**.
whatWouldHelp: Employers giving **time**, not a sudden letter.
